task: Hunt design-level contradictions in the exec-write protection (policies/p13_exec_write_paths.rego, policies/exec_analyze.py, policies/gate.sh integrity block). Every doubt needs file:line + why-it-matters.

subclaims.evidence: policies/exec_analyze.py:8-11,42-61; policies/p13_exec_write_paths.rego:29-50 — ana.ok==true suppresses the string fallback, and the analyzer empirically emits ok:true with empty writes for env/find/python3 -c/git rm/zsh -c/tar/curl -o/$(...)/cd-relative writes

policies/gate.sh:23-26 — find -maxdepth 1 excludes policies/.governance/* (policies.lock itself, tool-inventory.txt, current_phase); deleting policies.lock disables the check entirely; re-seal via cd-relative write bypasses P13

policies/gate.sh:5,67 — PATH is prepended with user-writable $HOME/.local/bin, so opa/python3/sha256sum/jq resolve to attacker-planted binaries; exec command can also feed non-string tool_input.command where jq -r and Rego replace() diverge

policies/gate.sh:26,67; policies/exec_analyze.py:6 — lock hashes file bytes only; analyzer's ok:true is trusted unconditionally, its runtime deps (python3, bashlex) are unsealed and resolved via the poisonable PATH

findings.text: cwd-relative write blind spot breaks the whole design AND enables a re-seal kill chain. `cd policies && rm p1.rego` → analyzer emits writes=["p1.rego"]; protected_hit needs substring 'policies/' so no deny, while ok:true suppresses the fallback. Same trick: `cd policies/.governance && echo HASH > policies.lock` → writes=["policies.lock"], which contains none of protected_paths (no 'policies/' prefix). Full chain: (1) `cd policies && sed -i ... exec_analyze.py` (missed), (2) sha256sum the tampered set (read-only, allowed), (3) `cd policies/.governance && printf HASH > policies.lock` (missed) → attacker-controlled analyzer + valid seal = silent permanent bypass. Verified empirically. Analyzer never tracks cwd; p13 only does substring match on literal word text.

PATH poisoning defeats both the policy engine and the integrity seal. gate.sh:5 prepends $HOME/.local/bin — a user-writable dir matched by NO protected_paths entry and no policy (grep-verified). `cp fake $HOME/.local/bin/opa` yields writes=["$HOME/.local/bin/opa"] → missed ($var + unlisted path). A planted opa echoing allow:true neuters every policy; planted sha256sum/find/cat make the lock check itself lie. Every gate dependency (opa:16,79; python3:67; sha256sum,find,cat,tr,sort,xargs,awk:24-26; jq,timeout) resolves through the poisoned PATH.

Analyzer verb/interpreter coverage gaps — all verified live to return ok:true,writes:[] (fallback then skipped): `env rm -rf policies/` (also nice/nohup/sudo/timeout/xargs wrappers), `find policies -exec rm {} +`, `python3 -c "open('policies/p1.rego','w')"` / `python -c`, `git rm policies/p1.rego`, `git pull` (GIT_WRITE_SUBS lacks rm/mv/pull/merge/rebase/cherry-pick/switch), `zsh -c`/`dash -c` (allowlist is only bash/sh/wsl), `wsl rm -rf` (only -c form recursed), `sh < pwn.sh`, `bash pwn.sh`, `tar xf`, `unzip -o`, `curl -o policies/x`, `eval`, `awk` system(). One structural layer miss = zero detection because ana.ok suppresses layer (b).

Windows .exe suffix defeats all verb matching. verb=os.path.basename(ws[0]) keeps the extension: `rm.exe -rf policies/`, `nc.exe`, `dd.exe`, `bash.exe -c`, `cmd.exe /c`, `powershell.exe -c` match nothing in WRITE_VERBS/blocked_commands/interpreter-allowlist. Deployment OS is Windows.

Command substitution and assignments are invisible to walk(). Verified: `x=$(rm -rf policies/)` → commands:[] writes:[] (the whole command vanishes — assignment node children never reached); `echo $(rm -rf policies/x)` → only 'echo' seen. MAX_DEPTH=3 prunes commandsubstitution subtrees before the inner command node is yielded.

bash -c recursion depth cap verified: MAX_DEPTH=3 → 4-deep `bash -c 'bash -c "bash -c \"bash -c rm...\""'` returns writes:[]. Also only the `-c` flag form recurses — `sh <script`, `bash script.sh`, `wsl cmd` all run arbitrary code unanalyzed.

Redirect operator coverage: only {">",">>","&>"} extracted. Verified `echo x <>policies/y` (read-write open) → writes:[]. `<` redirects are ignored entirely, hiding `sh < pwn.sh`. `>|`, `>&N` variants unhandled.

Lock find set excludes subdirectory runtime data. `find policies -maxdepth 1` (gate.sh:26) omits policies/.governance/tool-inventory.txt (feeds data.env.inventory → p5 recognized-tool check, lines 14-22: write '*' and any tool passes) and current_phase (feeds data.env.current_phase → p4_require_evidence phase math, lines 44-53). Mutating them never invalidates the seal. Worse: `rm policies/.governance/policies.lock` via any F1/F3 evasion makes the `[ -f ]` guard skip the integrity check entirely — seal self-disables. p4 protects .governance only for write/edit tools, not the exec path.

Claimed compensating control is false. p13 header says 'audit + policies.lock are the detection tier' for $var/eval/script evasion — but the lock only hashes policies/{*.rego,gate.sh,exec_analyze.py}. Evaded writes to approvals/, evidence/, state.md, tests.lock, .approved, logs/, src/ (all listed in protected_paths) have NO detection tier at all — they pass silently and no seal notices.

Integrity check is circular and self-referential. The seal pipeline itself (tr/find/sort/xargs/cat/sha256sum/awk, gate.sh:24-26) and the analyzer (python3 + unsealed bashlex import, exec_analyze.py:6) execute under the poisonable PATH — the tamper-detector runs on attacker-controlled tools. `[ -n "$EXP" ]` also means an empty policies.lock file silently skips the check. Nobody verifies the analyzer's ok:true claim — it is trusted input to data.env.exec_analysis.

No timeout and unbounded stdin on the analyzer. gate.sh:67 pipes the full command into python3 with no `timeout` (opa gets `timeout 4` at :79); exec_analyze.py:64 does unbounded sys.stdin.read(). A pathological/huge command hangs the pre-tool gate — DoS, or hook-timeout passthrough depending on harness behavior.

Over-deny false positive contradicts 'real write targets' claim: all non-flag args are counted as writes, so `cp policies/p1.rego /tmp/copy` (read-only copy) is denied — verified writes=["/tmp/copy","policies/p1.rego"]. Sources can't be distinguished from destinations; encourages operators to bypass/disable the layer.

bashlex dependency is undeclared and fails silently. exec_analyze.py:6 imports bashlex at top level (outside the try); no requirements file/pin exists. In this environment it raised ModuleNotFoundError until manually installed. Absence → non-zero exit → `|| echo '{}'` → exec_analysis={} → ok absent → permanent fallback-only mode with zero signal that the structural layer is dead.

env-trust divergence on non-string tool_input.command: gate.sh feeds `jq -r` output (stringified) to the analyzer, but Rego `replace(input.tool_input.command,...)` fails on non-strings, making both fallback rules undefined — analyzer and policy layers see different things. A non-string command is probably inert for a real exec tool, but the two-layer views can diverge on any input type mismatch or duplicate JSON keys.

Non-finding recorded to prevent false alarms: subdirectory .rego/.json injection under policies/ is loaded recursively by opa (p4:11-13 is correct), but added deny rules can only tighten; data.env overlap errors out → GOV_GATE_DOWN fail-closed. The maxdepth-1 lock gap bites only via .governance mutation (see finding), not via policy-file injection.
